screens.title: Understanding Performance Bottlenecks
screens.subtitle: Identifying and addressing slow points in your Azure applications.

narration.text: Every application, regardless of how well it's designed, can encounter performance bottlenecks. These are specific points in your system where the flow of data or execution slows down, impacting the overall responsiveness and efficiency. Common culprits include slow database queries, inefficient A P I calls, excessive network latency, or resource constraints like C P U, memory, or input and output. For instance, if your application frequently queries a large database without proper indexing, that database call becomes a bottleneck. The impact of these bottlenecks is significant: users experience delays, leading to frustration and potentially abandoning your application. From a business perspective, this can translate to lost sales or reduced productivity. Operationally, inefficient applications consume more resources, driving up your Azure costs. A key strategy to combat many of these issues is caching, which we'll explore next. Caching helps by storing frequently accessed data closer to the application, reducing the need to hit slower, more distant data sources repeatedly. This proactive approach to identifying and mitigating bottlenecks is fundamental to building high-performing cloud solutions. Understanding Performance Bottlenecks means slow performance degrades user experience, increases costs, and can be mitigated by identifying and optimizing critical paths, often starting with caching.. In practical terms, identifying and addressing slow points in your azure applications.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bottlenecks Impact Everything
keyIdea.text: Slow performance degrades user experience, increases costs, and can be mitigated by identifying and optimizing critical paths, often starting with caching.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.5›Performance Bottlenecks
What is a Bottleneck?

A Point of Congestion

A performance bottleneck is a component or process that limits the overall capacity or speed of an application. It's where the system's ability to process requests slows down.

Common Causes
  • Inefficient database queries
  • High network latency
  • Resource constraints (CPU, memory, I/O)
  • External API call delays
  • Suboptimal code execution
Key Takeaway

Identifying bottlenecks is the first step to optimization. Focus on areas with high latency or resource consumption.

Primary Solution

Introducing Caching

Caching stores frequently accessed data in a fast, temporary storage layer. This reduces the need to fetch data from slower sources like databases or external APIs, significantly improving responsiveness.

Faster Access

Data served from memory.

Reduced Load

Offloads primary data sources.

screens.title: Azure Cache for Redis: Fast Data Access
screens.subtitle: Leveraging an in-memory data store for enhanced application responsiveness.

narration.text: Azure Cache for Redis is a fully managed, in-memory data store service provided by Microsoft Azure. It's built on the popular open-source Redis, which stands for Remote Dictionary Server, and is renowned for its blazing-fast performance. Unlike traditional databases that store data on disk, Redis keeps data in R A M, allowing for extremely low-latency access. This makes it an ideal choice for scenarios where speed is paramount. For example, in a high-traffic e-commerce application, you can use Redis for data caching to store frequently accessed product catalogs or user profiles, reducing the load on your primary database and speeding up page loads. It's also excellent for managing user session state in web applications, especially when you have multiple instances of your application running, ensuring a seamless experience as users move between servers. Furthermore, Redis can act as a message broker for publish/subscribe patterns or distributed queues, enabling real-time communication between different parts of your application. Finally, it supports distributed locking, which is crucial for coordinating access to shared resources across multiple application instances, preventing race conditions and data corruption. Understanding these versatile capabilities is key to effectively integrating Azure Cache for Redis into your architecture.

keyIdea.title: Redis: Versatile Speed
keyIdea.text: Azure Cache for Redis is a high-performance, in-memory data store with diverse applications beyond simple caching, including session management and messaging.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.5›Azure Cache for Redis
Core Definition

Azure Cache for Redis

A fully managed, in-memory data store based on the popular open-source Redis, offering high-speed data access.

Use Case 1

Data Caching

Store frequently accessed database queries or API responses.

Use Case 2

Session State

Manage user session data for scaled-out web applications.

Use Case 3

Message Broker

Implement publish/subscribe patterns or distributed queues.

Use Case 4

Distributed Locking

Coordinate access to shared resources across instances.

Key Takeaway

Azure Cache for Redis offers a versatile, high-speed, in-memory solution for various performance-critical application needs.

screens.title: Integrating Redis into Your Application
screens.subtitle: Steps to provision and connect Azure Cache for Redis.

narration.text: Now that we understand what Azure Cache for Redis is, let's look at how to integrate it into your application. The process typically involves three main steps. First, you need to provision an Azure Cache for Redis instance in the Azure portal or via CLI. This sets up the dedicated in-memory store in your chosen Azure region. Second, you'll install a Redis client library in your application. For. NET applications, Stack Exchange. Redis is a popular choice, while Node. js developers might use ioredis. These libraries provide the necessary APIs to interact with the Redis cache. Finally, and most critically, you'll modify your application code. This involves implementing a 'cache-aside' pattern: before making a potentially slow call to your primary data source, your code first checks if the data is already in the Redis cache. If it is, you retrieve it directly, saving time and resources. If not, you fetch the data from the original source, store it in the cache for future requests, and then return it to the user. This pattern ensures that frequently requested data becomes readily available, significantly boosting your application's responsiveness. The C# example on the right illustrates this logic for retrieving product data.

keyIdea.title: Cache-Aside Pattern
keyIdea.text: Implement Redis by provisioning, adding a client library, and modifying code to check the cache before hitting the primary data source.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.5›Redis Implementation
Implementation Steps
  1. Provision Redis Instance: Create an Azure Cache for Redis resource in your Azure subscription.
  2. Install Client Library: Add a Redis client library (e.g., StackExchange.Redis for .NET) to your application project.
  3. Modify Application Code: Implement logic to check the cache first, then the primary data source, and finally store results in the cache.
Example Scenario

Caching Product Details

An e-commerce API retrieves product information. By caching product details, subsequent requests for the same product are served much faster, reducing database load.

Key Takeaway

The 'cache-aside' pattern is fundamental: check cache, if not found, fetch from source, then cache and return.

C# Code Example: ProductService
public class ProductService
{
    private readonly IDatabase _cache;
    // Assume _dbContext is your database context

    public ProductService(IConnectionMultiplexer redis)
    {
        _cache = redis.GetDatabase();
    }

    public async Task<Product> GetProductByIdAsync(string productId)
    {
        string cacheKey = $"product:{productId}";

        // Try to get from cache
        string cachedProductJson = await _cache.StringGetAsync(cacheKey);
        if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(cachedProductJson))
        {
            return JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Product>(cachedProductJson);
        }

        // Fetch from database (simulated)
        Product product = await _dbContext.Products.FirstOrDefaultAsync(p => p.Id == productId);

        if (product != null)
        {
            // Store in cache for 5 minutes
            await _cache.StringSetAsync(cacheKey, JsonSerializer.Serialize(product), TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5));
        }

        return product;
    }
}

screens.title: Ensuring Data Freshness with Cache Invalidation
screens.subtitle: Preventing stale data from impacting user experience.

narration.text: While caching dramatically improves performance, it introduces a new challenge: ensuring the cached data remains fresh. If data in the cache becomes outdated, users might see stale or incorrect information, which can lead to confusion and distrust. This is where cache invalidation strategies become critical. One common approach is time-based expiration, where you set a specific time-to-live, or TTL, for cached items, like five minutes in our previous example. After this period, the item is automatically removed from the cache, forcing a fresh fetch from the primary source. Another strategy is event-driven invalidation. Here, when the underlying data in the database changes, an event is triggered that explicitly clears or updates the corresponding item in the cache. For instance, if a product's price is updated, an event could invalidate that product's entry in Redis. More advanced patterns include write-through or write-behind, where data is written to both the cache and the primary data store simultaneously or asynchronously. A common mistake is not having any invalidation strategy, leading to persistent stale data. Choosing the right strategy depends on your application's tolerance for staleness and the frequency of data changes. Implementing a robust invalidation strategy is just as important as implementing caching itself.

keyIdea.title: Freshness is Key
keyIdea.text: Cache invalidation ensures data consistency by removing or updating stale cached items, preventing users from seeing outdated information.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.5›Cache Invalidation

Ensuring Data Freshness with Cache Invalidation

Preventing stale data from impacting user experience.

Time-Based Expiration

Data automatically expires after a set duration (TTL).

Event-Driven Invalidation

Cache cleared or updated when source data changes.

Write-Through/Behind

Data written to cache and primary store simultaneously.

Common Mistake

No Invalidation Strategy

Failing to implement any cache invalidation can lead to users consistently seeing outdated information, eroding trust and causing data inconsistencies. Always consider how and when your cached data should be refreshed.

Key Takeaway

A robust cache invalidation strategy is as vital as caching itself to maintain data consistency and user trust.

screens.title: Accelerating Content with Azure CDN
screens.subtitle: Delivering static assets quickly to users worldwide.

narration.text: For applications serving static content like images, C S S, JavaScript files, or videos to a global audience, Content Delivery Networks, or CDNs, are indispensable. An Azure CDN works by caching your static content at strategically located points-of-presence, or PoPs, around the world. Think of these PoPs as mini-data centers positioned close to your users. When a user requests content, instead of fetching it from your origin server, which might be thousands of miles away, the CDN serves it from the nearest PoP. This significantly reduces network latency, which is the time it takes for data to travel, and dramatically improves page load times. For example, if your website is hosted in the US but a user in Europe accesses it, the CDN ensures that static assets are served from a European PoP, making the experience much faster. Beyond speed, CDNs also offload traffic from your origin server, reducing its workload and improving its overall performance and stability. This not only enhances the user experience but also contributes to the resilience and cost-efficiency of your application. CDNs are a cornerstone of modern web architecture for global applications.

keyIdea.title: CDN: Edge Delivery
keyIdea.text: Azure CDN caches static content at global edge locations (PoPs) to reduce latency, accelerate delivery, and offload origin servers, improving user experience worldwide.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.5›Azure CDN
What is Azure CDN?

Global Content Caching

Azure CDN caches static content (images, CSS, JS, videos) at Points-of-Presence (PoPs) worldwide. Content is served from the nearest PoP to the user.

Key Benefits
  • Reduced Latency: Content served from closer locations.
  • Faster Page Loads: Improves overall user experience.
  • Offloads Origin Server: Reduces traffic and workload on your primary server.
  • Improved Scalability: Handles traffic spikes more effectively.
Key Takeaway

Azure CDN is crucial for global applications, delivering static content rapidly and efficiently to users everywhere.

User Request

CDN PoP (Cached)
Origin Server (Database)

screens.title: Configuring Azure CDN for Your Application
screens.subtitle: Steps to integrate CDN endpoints for static content delivery.

narration.text: Implementing Azure CDN is a straightforward process that can yield significant performance gains. The first step is to create a CDN profile and endpoint within Azure. The profile acts as a collection of CDN endpoints, and each endpoint specifies the origin from which content will be pulled. Your origin could be an Azure Storage account, an Azure Web App, or even a custom origin like an on-premises web server. Once your CDN endpoint is configured and pointing to your origin, the crucial next step is to update your application's URLs. Instead of directly referencing your origin server for static assets, you'll modify your H T M L, C S S, or JavaScript to use the CDN endpoint's URL. For example, an image tag that previously pointed to your web app's domain would now point to your CDN endpoint's domain. A common mistake here is not configuring proper cache-control headers on your origin. Without these, the CDN might not cache content effectively or could serve stale content. Another pitfall is attempting to cache dynamic, user-specific content, which can lead to incorrect data being displayed. Always ensure you're caching only static, publicly accessible assets. By following these steps, you can leverage Azure CDN to deliver a faster, more responsive experience to your global user base.

keyIdea.title: CDN URL Rewriting
keyIdea.text: Integrate Azure CDN by creating a profile and endpoint, then updating application URLs to serve static assets from the CDN endpoint, ensuring proper cache-control headers.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.5›CDN Configuration
CDN Implementation Steps
  1. Create CDN Profile & Endpoint: Define your CDN profile and an endpoint pointing to your origin (e.g., Azure Storage, Web App).
  2. Update Application URLs: Modify your application's code to reference the CDN endpoint for static assets instead of the origin.
  3. Configure Cache-Control: Ensure your origin server sends appropriate Cache-Control headers for effective caching.
Common CDN Mistakes
  • Not configuring proper Cache-Control headers on the origin.
  • Attempting to cache dynamic or user-specific content.
  • Forgetting to update all static asset URLs to use the CDN.
Key Takeaway

Proper CDN integration involves creating endpoints and updating asset URLs, coupled with correct cache-control settings on the origin.

HTML Code Example: Before & After CDN
<!-- Before CDN -->
<img src="https://mywebapp.azurewebsites.net/images/logo.png" />

<!-- After CDN -->
<img src="https://mycdnendpoint.azureedge.net/images/logo.png" />

<!-- CSS Example -->
.hero-background {
  background-image: url('https://mycdnendpoint.azureedge.net/css/hero.jpg');
}

screens.title: Scaling Your Azure Resources
screens.subtitle: Choosing between vertical and horizontal scaling for demand management.

narration.text: Scaling is the process of adjusting the resources allocated to your application to effectively meet varying levels of demand. It's a fundamental concept in cloud computing, allowing your applications to remain performant and available without overspending on idle resources. There are two primary types of scaling: vertical and horizontal. Vertical scaling, also known as 'scaling up' or 'scaling down,' involves increasing or decreasing the size of an existing resource. For example, upgrading an Azure App Service plan from a Basic tier to a Standard tier provides more C P U and memory to a single instance. While simple to implement, vertical scaling has inherent limits; you can only scale up so much, and it often requires downtime for the changes to take effect. In contrast, horizontal scaling, or 'scaling out' and 'scaling in,' involves adding or removing instances of a resource. Imagine adding more App Service instances to handle increased web traffic. This approach is generally preferred for stateless applications because it offers superior elasticity and fault tolerance. If one instance fails, others can continue serving requests. Horizontal scaling allows your application to handle much larger loads by distributing them across multiple, smaller resources. Understanding the differences and when to apply each is crucial for designing a resilient and cost-effective cloud architecture.

keyIdea.title: Scaling for Demand
keyIdea.text: Scaling adjusts resources to meet demand, with vertical scaling increasing instance size and horizontal scaling adding more instances, the latter often preferred for cloud elasticity.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.5›Scaling Strategies

Scaling Your Azure Resources

Choosing between vertical and horizontal scaling for demand management.

Vertical Scaling (Scale Up/Down)

Adjusting Resource Size

  • Definition: Increasing or decreasing the size (CPU, memory) of an existing resource.
  • Example: Upgrading an App Service plan from Basic to Standard.
  • Pros: Simpler to manage for single instances.
  • Cons: Finite limits, often requires downtime, can be more expensive for peak loads.
Analogy: Bigger Car

Replacing a small car with a larger one to carry more passengers.

Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out/In)

Adjusting Resource Instances

  • Definition: Adding or removing instances of a resource.
  • Example: Adding more App Service instances to a web farm.
  • Pros: Better elasticity, fault tolerance, cost-effective for fluctuating loads.
  • Cons: Requires stateless applications or shared state management.
Analogy: More Cars

Adding more small cars to carry more passengers simultaneously.

Key Takeaway

Horizontal scaling is generally preferred in cloud environments for its elasticity and fault tolerance, especially for stateless applications.

screens.title: Automating Resource Adjustment with Auto-scaling
screens.subtitle: Dynamically matching application resources to demand.

narration.text: Building on the concept of horizontal scaling, auto-scaling takes resource management to the next level by automating the process. Auto-scaling automatically adjusts the number of instances of your application based on predefined rules and metrics, such as C P U utilization, memory usage, or queue length. This is incredibly efficient because your application dynamically scales out during peak demand to maintain performance and then scales in during low periods to save costs. For example, you can configure an Azure App Service to scale out and add more instances when its C P U usage exceeds 70% for five minutes, ensuring your users don't experience slowdowns. Conversely, it can scale in and remove instances when C P U drops below 30% for ten minutes, preventing you from paying for idle resources. The Azure CLI example on the right demonstrates how to set up such rules. When configuring auto-scaling, it's vital to ensure your application is stateless or uses a shared state mechanism, like Azure Cache for Redis, so that multiple instances can handle requests correctly without losing user data. Also, define appropriate 'cool-down' periods to prevent 'flapping,' which is rapid scaling up and down, as this can be inefficient and costly. Auto-scaling is a powerful tool for optimizing both performance and cost, but it requires careful planning and monitoring.

keyIdea.title: Smart Resource Management
keyIdea.text: Auto-scaling dynamically adjusts resources based on metrics, optimizing performance and cost, but requires stateless applications and careful rule configuration.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.5›Auto-scaling
What is Auto-scaling?

Dynamic Resource Adjustment

Automatically adjusts the number of instances for your application based on predefined metrics and rules. This ensures optimal performance during peak loads and cost savings during low demand.

Key Considerations
  • Stateless Applications: Ideal for horizontal scaling.
  • Shared State: Use services like Azure Cache for Redis for stateful scenarios.
  • Cool-down Periods: Prevent 'flapping' (rapid scale up/down).
  • Metric Selection: Choose relevant metrics (CPU, memory, queue length).
Key Takeaway

Auto-scaling optimizes resource usage and cost, but requires careful configuration and consideration of application state.

Azure CLI Example: App Service Auto-scale
# Create auto-scale setting
az monitor autoscale create \
    --resource-group "MonitorDemoRG" \
    --resource "cohortia-demo-app-YOUR_UNIQUE_NAME" \
    --resource-type Microsoft.Web/sites \
    --name "WebAppAutoScale" \
    --min-count 1 \
    --max-count 5 \
    --count 1 \
    --location "eastus" \
    --enabled true

# Add scale-out rule (CPU > 70%)
az monitor autoscale rule create \
    --resource-group "MonitorDemoRG" \
    --autoscale-name "WebAppAutoScale" \
    --condition "MetricName eq 'CpuPercentage' and GreaterThan or Equal '70'" \
    --scale out 1 \
    --cooldown 5m \
    --time-aggregation Average \
    --metric-namespace Microsoft.Web/sites \
    --metric-resource-id $APP_SERVICE_ID \
    --description "Scale out when CPU > 70%"

# Add scale-in rule (CPU < 30%)
az monitor autoscale rule create \
    --resource-group "MonitorDemoRG" \
    --autoscale-name "WebAppAutoScale" \
    --condition "MetricName eq 'CpuPercentage' and LessThan or Equal '30'" \
    --scale in 1 \
    --cooldown 10m \
    --time-aggregation Average \
    --metric-namespace Microsoft.Web/sites \
    --metric-resource-id $APP_SERVICE_ID \
    --description "Scale in when CPU < 30%"

screens.title: Understanding Serverless Cold Starts
screens.subtitle: Addressing initial latency in Azure Functions.

narration.text: Serverless architectures, like Azure Functions, offer incredible benefits in terms of scalability and cost-efficiency, but they come with a unique performance challenge known as 'cold starts.' A cold start occurs when an instance of your function app needs to be initialized from scratch after a period of inactivity. This initialization process involves several steps: Azure needs to find your function code, load the runtime environment, and then load all its dependencies. Imagine a restaurant that only prepares a dish when a customer orders it, and it has to gather all ingredients and set up the kitchen each time. This setup time is the cold start. For serverless functions, this can introduce a noticeable delay, often several seconds, for the very first request after a period of quiet. While subsequent requests to an already 'warmed' instance are fast, this initial latency can significantly impact user experience, especially for interactive applications or HTTP-triggered functions where immediate response is expected. For example, a user clicking a button that triggers an Azure Function might experience a delay if that function hasn't been invoked recently. Understanding this inherent characteristic of serverless is the first step to effectively mitigating its impact.

keyIdea.title: Cold Start: Initial Delay
keyIdea.text: Serverless cold starts are initial delays caused by on-demand instance initialization, impacting responsiveness for the first request after inactivity.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.5›Cold Starts
Core Definition

Serverless Cold Start

The delay experienced when a serverless function instance needs to be initialized from scratch after a period of inactivity.

Cause 1

Code & Runtime Loading

Function code and runtime environment must be loaded into memory.

Cause 2

Dependency Initialization

External libraries and connections need to be established.

Impact

Increased Latency

First requests after inactivity experience noticeable delays.

Analogy

Restaurant Setup

Kitchen setup time before the first dish is prepared.

Key Takeaway

Cold starts are an inherent trade-off in serverless, causing initial latency due to on-demand resource provisioning.

screens.title: Strategies to Reduce Cold Start Latency
screens.subtitle: Practical approaches for faster serverless function execution.

narration.text: While cold starts are a characteristic of serverless, there are several effective strategies to mitigate their impact and improve the responsiveness of your Azure Functions. One of the most direct solutions is to use a Premium Plan, also known as Elastic Premium. This plan offers 'pre-warmed' instances, meaning Azure keeps function instances ready, significantly reducing cold start times. If your function app is hosted on an App Service Plan, enabling 'Always On' will keep the app loaded, preventing cold starts altogether, though this isn't applicable to the Consumption Plan. For all plans, minimizing dependencies in your function code is crucial. The fewer external libraries and modules your function needs to load, the faster it will initialize. Consider using deployment slots for HTTP-triggered functions; you can 'warm up' a new version in a staging slot before swapping it into production, ensuring users hit an already active instance. The choice of language also matters: pre-compiled languages like C# generally have faster cold starts than interpreted languages like Python or Node. js. Finally, for less critical functions, you can set up a timer-triggered function or an external service to periodically 'ping' your HTTP-triggered functions, keeping them warm. By combining these strategies, you can significantly reduce the perceived latency of cold starts and deliver a more consistent user experience.

keyIdea.title: Mitigating Cold Starts
keyIdea.text: Reduce serverless cold start latency through Premium Plans, 'Always On' settings, minimal dependencies, deployment slots, pre-compiled languages, and periodic 'pings'.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.5›Cold Start Mitigation

Strategies to Reduce Cold Start Latency

Practical approaches for faster serverless function execution.

Plan-Based Solutions

Premium & Always On

  • Premium Plan: Offers pre-warmed instances.
  • Always On: Keeps App Service Plan functions loaded (not for Consumption).
Code & Deployment

Lean Code & Warm-up

  • Minimal Dependencies: Reduces load time.
  • Deployment Slots: Warm up new versions before swap.
  • Pre-compiled Languages: Faster initialization (e.g., C# over Python).
Proactive Warming

Periodic Pinging

  • Dummy Requests: Periodically invoke functions to keep them warm.
  • Timer Triggers: Use a timer function to ping HTTP functions.
Key Takeaway

A multi-faceted approach, combining plan choices, code optimization, and proactive warming, is most effective for cold start mitigation.

screens.title: Essential Performance Optimization Terms
screens.subtitle: Reinforcing core concepts for building high-performance Azure solutions.

narration.text: We've covered several critical concepts for optimizing Azure solution performance. First, remember that caching is about storing frequently accessed data in a fast, temporary layer to reduce latency and improve overall responsiveness. This is a fundamental technique for speeding up data retrieval. Azure Cache for Redis is a prime example of this, offering a fully managed, in-memory data store that's incredibly versatile for caching, session state, and even messaging. It's a powerful tool in your optimization toolkit. Finally, we discussed cache invalidation, which refers to the strategies you employ to ensure your cached data remains fresh and consistent with the original source. Without proper invalidation, your users could be presented with outdated information, undermining the benefits of caching. Mastering these three concepts provides a strong foundation for building performant applications.

screens.title: Advanced Performance Concepts
screens.subtitle: Key takeaways for scaling and serverless optimization.

narration.text: Continuing our recap, we explored Content Delivery Networks, or CDNs. These are distributed networks of servers that cache static content closer to users, dramatically reducing latency and offloading your origin servers. CDNs are vital for global applications. We then delved into scaling, which is the process of adjusting resources to meet demand. We distinguished between vertical scaling, which increases the size of a single resource, and horizontal scaling, which adds more instances. Auto-scaling automates this process based on predefined rules, ensuring optimal performance and cost-efficiency. Finally, we addressed serverless cold starts, the initial delay experienced by serverless functions when an instance needs to be initialized from scratch. We learned various strategies to mitigate this, ensuring a more consistent and responsive serverless experience. These concepts collectively empower you to design and manage highly performant, scalable, and cost-effective Azure solutions.

keyIdea.text: CDNs, intelligent scaling, and cold start mitigation are crucial for global reach, dynamic resource management, and responsive serverless applications.
